summary:
A.C.R.E (Agricultural Climate Replay Engine) is a free web app that lets a farmer test a crop plan before spending a season on it. The grower draws a field on a satellite map anywhere on Earth, says what they grow and when, and the app replays that plan through every season NASA has recorded for that exact place since 1981.

It answers three questions in plain sentences: how often was planting time too dry, how much rain fell on bare ground, and how much money does the plan leave. The grower can then try other plans, such as adding a cover crop or a second crop, and compare them under the same weather.

It addresses the Field Shift challenge by turning 45 years of NASA weather and soil wetness data into a decision a farmer can act on. This matters because most of the world's farms are small, and few growers have a way to see how a plan holds up across good and bad years. A.C.R.E needs no account, no sensors and no forecast, and every number on screen says where it came from.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
A.C.R.E is one guided sequence of six steps, written for a farmer and not for a data scientist.
1. Your farm: search any town and draw your field on a satellite map.
2. What you do now: your crops, planting and harvest dates, equipment, prices and how bad a bad year is, one short question at a time.
3. Simulate: your plan is replayed about 200 times over the next 10 years, using the real weather recorded for your field.
4. Try other plans: plans suggested for your place, or your own.
5. Compare: every plan side by side, under the same weather.
6. Your 10-year plan: dated and printable.

HOW IT WORKS
When a field is drawn, our service fetches the NASA POWER daily record for that spot, which is built on NASA's MERRA-2 reanalysis, from 1981 to today: rain, soil wetness at the surface and in the root zone, and air temperature. That is more than 16,000 daily records for one field. The engine builds possible 10-year futures from those real years and runs the grower's plan through each one. The answer comes first in plain sentences, for example "2 of 10 years were too dry in the weeks before planting", with all the numbers one click away. It is a replay of recorded weather, not a forecast.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT
Smarter decisions: a plan is tested against real weather before a season is spent on it.
Soil and water: the app shows how much rain falls on bare ground under each plan, which is the case for keeping fields covered.
Works anywhere: we ran it from start to finish for fields in Kenya, India, Germany, Brazil, Argentina and the United States. It covers farms worked by hand, with animals or with a tractor, and prices can be entered in any currency.
Honest by design: every number says where it came from, a missing number stays blank instead of showing zero, and nothing is presented as a forecast.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE
Most climate tools show charts of the past. A.C.R.E asks the question a farmer actually has, "will my plan hold up?", and answers it by replaying the field's own weather history with the grower's own crops and dates.

TOOLS WE USED
Web app: React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre for the map, three.js for the 3D field. Service: Python and FastAPI. Data: NASA POWER and MERRA-2, plus the open data listed below. AI coding assistants (Claude and Codex) helped write and test code under our direction. Inside the app, an AI model is used only to look up published crop facts, and those are always labelled as found by AI and never shown as verified.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED
The limits are stated in the app. One weather square is about 50 km across. Typical planting dates come from a global dataset from the 1990s. Checked local guidance exists only for North Carolina so far. Money results need the grower's own prices and costs where no published figures exist. Next on our list: more languages, a phone layout, local currencies and a this-season to-do list.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources), agroclimatology daily data
NASA POWER Daily API (rain, soil wetness and air temperature variables)
NASA MERRA-2 reanalysis (Global Modeling and Assimilation Office)
projectRefs: SAGE crop calendar dataset (Sacks et al. 2010), typical planting and harvest dates
USDA NRCS Soil Data Access (US soils)
USDA NASS Quick Stats (US yields and prices)
USDA ERS Commodity Costs and Returns
FAOSTAT (FAO), world crop prices and yields
OpenRouter (AI model access for in-app crop fact lookups)
Claude Code by Anthropic (AI coding assistant)
